prompt: How does Go's CPU profiler find out where the time went?
hint: Think of what it writes down, and how often.

choices.text: It times every call on the way in and on the way out
choices.why: That is a tracer's approach, and its cost grows with the number of calls. The profiler never times a call.

choices.text: A hundred times a second it records the running stack
choices.why: Right. Each sample stands for 10 ms, and a function in many samples is where the time went, however many calls that took.

choices.text: It counts calls and multiplies by an average cost per function
choices.why: A CPU profile holds no call counts at all; it holds stacks and the number of ticks each was seen at.

choices.text: The compiler inserts a counter at the top of every function
choices.why: That is how coverage works, not profiling. A profile needs no special build.

prompt: A service's memory grows a little every day until it is restarted. Which view of the heap profile answers "what is holding it"?
hint: One pair of views is about now, the other about the whole life of the process.

choices.text: `alloc_space`
choices.why: That counts everything ever allocated, garbage included. A program that churns looks huge there even when nothing stays.

choices.text: `alloc_objects`
choices.why: Also since the start of the program, counted in allocations. It finds churn, not retention.

choices.text: `inuse_space`
choices.why: Right. It is the bytes still live, by the stack that allocated them: where a leak shows.

choices.text: the `threadcreate` profile
choices.why: That records where operating system threads were started, which is rarely where memory goes.

prompt: A program never calls `runtime.SetBlockProfileRate`. What does its `block` profile hold?
hint: Section 05 shows the count beside it.

choices.text: Nothing: blocking is not recorded until the program asks
choices.why: Right. Recording every wait would slow the programs that need the profile, so it starts off, and the index page showed it at 0.

choices.text: One sample per 512 KB of blocking
choices.why: 512 KB is the heap profiler's rate, `runtime.MemProfileRate`. Blocking is measured in time, and here not at all.

choices.text: Every channel operation, because the default rate is 1
choices.why: A rate of 1 records every event, but the default is off; only a call to `SetBlockProfileRate` turns it on.

choices.text: Mutex waits only; channels belong to the goroutine profile
choices.why: The block profile covers channels, mutexes and `WaitGroup` alike. It is simply off.

prompt: A tick of the CPU profiler every 10 milliseconds is a rate of 100 ___.
hint: The unit of samples per second.

prompt: Why does `BenchmarkCount` read `testdata/access.log` before `for b.Loop()` rather than inside it?
hint: What would the time per iteration include otherwise?

choices.text: So that reading the disk is not part of what is timed
choices.why: Right. `b.Loop` resets the timer on its first call, so the setup before it is excluded and only counting is measured.

choices.text: Because a test may not open files inside the loop
choices.why: Nothing forbids it; it would only measure the disk along with the code.

choices.text: So the go command can cache the file between runs
choices.why: The go command caches test results, not files a benchmark reads, and benchmarks are not cached at all.

choices.text: `b.SetBytes` only works with data read before the loop
choices.why: `SetBytes` just records a number used for the MB/s column; it does not care where the data came from.

prompt: `BenchmarkCount` counted a 100,000-line log and reported `200009 allocs/op`. How many allocations is that per line, to the nearest whole number?
hint: Divide, and ignore the handful left over.

prompt: `go tool pprof -top mem.out` on the file `go test -memprofile` wrote says `Type: alloc_space`. Why not `inuse_space`, the heap profile's usual default?
hint: Which profile does the test binary write?

choices.text: pprof always opens memory profiles on `alloc_space`
choices.why: A heap profile from `WriteHeapProfile` opened on `inuse_space` in section 04. The default depends on the profile.

choices.text: The benchmark freed everything, so `inuse_space` was empty and pprof switched
choices.why: pprof does not switch views on its own; an empty view is shown as empty, as in section 04.

choices.text: `go test` writes the `allocs` profile
choices.why: Right. It holds the same records as `heap`, with `alloc_space` marked as the default, `[dflt]` in the `-raw` header.

choices.text: `-benchmem` turns off the live-heap records
choices.why: `-benchmem` only adds the B/op and allocs/op columns; the `-raw` header still listed all four values.

prompt: The benchmark's CPU profile holds 120 samples. A function shows 0.03s flat. What can you safely conclude about it?

choices.text: It takes 2.5% of the time, give or take a tenth of a percent
choices.why: Three ticks out of 120 cannot carry that precision; one tick more or less moves it by almost a point.

choices.text: It is called three times per benchmark iteration
choices.why: A CPU profile counts ticks, not calls. Three ticks say nothing about how often it ran.

choices.text: It is small, and its rank among the small ones is noise
choices.why: Right. 0.03 s is three samples; a longer run such as `-benchtime 5s` is how to rank functions that size.

choices.text: It never appears in the call graph of `tally.Count`
choices.why: Nothing about three samples says where in the stacks they were; it may well sit under `Count`.

prompt: Why does `profcount` put its work in `run`, which returns an error, instead of calling `log.Fatal` inside `main` when something fails?
hint: What happens to deferred calls when a program exits through `os.Exit`?

choices.text: `log.Fatal` cannot print to standard error while the profiler is running
choices.why: It prints fine. The trouble is what it skips after printing.

choices.text: `os.Exit` skips the deferred `StopCPUProfile`, so the file stays empty
choices.why: Right. `log.Fatal` calls `os.Exit`, deferred calls never run, the profile is never finished, and pprof has nothing to read.

choices.text: `run` is faster, because `main` is not optimised
choices.why: `main` is compiled like any other function. The reason is the defers.

choices.text: A profile can only be written from a function that returns an error
choices.why: `StartCPUProfile` works anywhere; it needs `StopCPUProfile` to run before the program ends.

prompt: The heap profile of `profcount`, on its default view, showed 2.2 MB live and none of it from `tally`. What does that say?
hint: Look at when the profile was written, and what `Count` keeps.

choices.text: The heap profile was broken by the CPU profile running at the same time
choices.why: Both profiles were fine; the live heap really was the profiler's buffer and the runtime's own.

choices.text: `Count` allocates almost nothing, so it cannot be the problem
choices.why: The `alloc_space` view of the same file showed 255.18 MB allocated by `Count`'s callees. Little is kept; a lot is made.

choices.text: `runtime.GC()` deleted `tally`'s records from the profile
choices.why: A collection marks a record's objects as freed; the record stays and still counts in the `alloc` views.

choices.text: Everything `Count` made was garbage and had been collected
choices.why: Right. `inuse_space` answers what holds memory now, and after `runtime.GC()` nothing of the count was left.

prompt: Counting the 2,000,000-line log allocated 255.18 MB in total, where pprof's MB is 1,048,576 bytes. About how many bytes is that per line?
Put the steps of `profcount`'s `run` in the order they happen when both profiles are asked for.
hint: Deferred calls run last, in reverse.
items: `runtime.GC()` brings the heap records up to date
the deferred `pprof.StopCPUProfile` finishes the CPU profile

prompt: What does the blank import `_ "net/http/pprof"` do in `profserve`?
hint: The program uses no name from the package.

choices.text: It registers the `/debug/pprof/` handlers on `http.DefaultServeMux`
choices.why: Right. Its `init` adds the handlers, and `ListenAndServe(addr, nil)` serves that default mux.

choices.text: It starts a web server on port 6060
choices.why: The import starts nothing; the program's own goroutine calls `ListenAndServe` on the address from `-pprof`.

choices.text: It turns on the block and mutex profiles
choices.why: The index page still showed `block` and `mutex` at 0; those need `SetBlockProfileRate` and `SetMutexProfileFraction`.

choices.text: Nothing until the program calls `pprof.Handler`
choices.why: The handlers exist from the moment the package is initialised; `profserve` never calls anything in it.

prompt: Thirty goroutines of `profserve` sat on `main.go:50`, `done <- result{s, err}`, in state `chan send`. Why could none of them ever finish?

choices.text: The channel was closed, and a send on a closed channel blocks
choices.why: A send on a closed channel panics; it does not wait. Nobody closed `done`.

choices.text: The timeout returned and left an unbuffered channel with no receiver
choices.why: Right. `countBefore` had already returned through the timer, so the send waits for a receiver that no longer exists.

choices.text: The counts were still reading the file
choices.why: `chan send` is the state of a goroutine that finished its work and is trying to hand over the result.

choices.text: `time.After` holds the channel until its timer fires again
choices.why: `time.After` returns a channel of its own; it has nothing to do with `done`.

prompt: The fix gave the channel room for one value: `done := make(chan result, ___)`.
A service already serves its public API with `http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil)`. A colleague adds `import _ "net/http/pprof"`. Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: Which mux does `nil` mean, and what is now on it?

choices.text: `/debug/pprof/` is now reachable by anybody who can reach port 8080
choices.why: Right. The import registered on `DefaultServeMux`, and `nil` serves exactly that mux on the public port.

choices.text: A stranger can read the process's command line from `cmdline`
choices.why: Right. `cmdline` returns the arguments the process was started with, secrets included if any were passed that way.

choices.text: The handlers ask for a password the first time they are used
choices.why: They have no authentication of any kind.

choices.text: Moving the profiles to a separate listener on 127.0.0.1 fixes it, with the public API on a mux of its own
choices.why: Right. The public server gets `http.NewServeMux()`, and the default mux, with the profiles, listens only on loopback.

prompt: Match each question about a Go program with the profile that answers it.
hint: One of the descriptions on the right matches no profile in the lesson.

pairs.left: Which code is using the processor?
What is keeping memory alive right now?
Which goroutines can never run again?
Where do goroutines wait on channels and locks?

prompt: A batch job takes forty minutes and you cannot change its code today, only its command line and environment. It already imports nothing from `runtime/pprof` or `net/http/pprof`. Which way of taking a profile from this lesson is left?
hint: Each of the three ways needed something in the program or its tests.

choices.text: Fetch `/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30` while it runs
choices.why: Nothing serves that path: the handlers exist only in a program that imports `net/http/pprof` and listens.

choices.text: Run `go tool pprof` on the binary with `-seconds 30`
choices.why: `go tool pprof` reads profiles; it cannot make a program that does not profile itself produce one.

choices.text: None of the three; a benchmark of its core function is the way in
choices.why: Right. Two of the ways need code in the program; a benchmark with `-cpuprofile` needs only a test file next to the code, which measures the function rather than the job.

choices.text: Set `GODEBUG=cpuprofile=1` and read the file it leaves
choices.why: There is no such setting; a CPU profile is started by `StartCPUProfile` or by the test binary's `-cpuprofile`.

prompt: Three profiles in this lesson, of a benchmark, of `profcount` and of `profserve`, put the same function at the top. Which one, and why does the agreement matter?
hint: Two different programs, two different inputs.

choices.text: `tally.Count`, because it is called first
choices.why: `Count` has almost no time of its own; it was high only in the sense of being on nearly every stack.

choices.text: `strings.Fields`, by three measurements
choices.why: Right. A benchmark, a whole program and a running service all ranked it first, which is what makes it worth fixing in lesson 13.

choices.text: `runtime.asyncPreempt`, which shows the scheduler is the bottleneck
choices.why: It appeared in some runs but was not first in all three, and it is the runtime interrupting goroutines, not the cause of the work.

choices.text: `time.Parse`, since every line has a timestamp
choices.why: Every line also has five fields to split; `time.Parse` was a few percent in each profile.
